entities.name: Anselm of Laon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Anselm of Laon (c. 1050 – 1117), a preeminent French theologian and scholar, established the influential School of Laon, which became a pivotal center for the development of systematic theology and biblical exegesis in the early 12th century. His intellectual leadership, particularly in the nascent Scholastic movement, profoundly shaped the methods of scriptural interpretation and doctrinal synthesis that would define high medieval thought, bridging the gap between monastic learning and the emerging university model. He is often recognized alongside figures like William of Champeaux and Peter Abelard as foundational to the intellectual ferment of the era, attracting students from across Western Europe to his innovative pedagogical approach.

Born in Laon, Anselm initially studied under Manegold of Lautenbach and later, controversially, under Anselm of Canterbury in Bec. Returning to Laon around 1080, he began teaching at the cathedral school, attracting a vast number of students who sought his instruction in theology and biblical studies. His primary contribution lay in the *Glossa Ordinaria*, a monumental compilation of patristic and earlier medieval commentaries on the Bible, meticulously arranged as interlinear and marginal glosses. While not solely his work, Anselm and his brother Ralph were instrumental in its development, organization, and dissemination, establishing a standardized format for biblical study.
